content: Large doses of methenamine, specifically 8 grams daily for a duration of 3 to 4 weeks, have been associated with adverse effects such as bladder irritation, painful and frequent urination, the presence of albumin in the urine (albuminuria), and visible blood in the urine (gross hematuria). Prescribing methenamine hippurate tablets USP without a confirmed or strongly suspected bacterial infection, or without a clear prophylactic indication, is unlikely to benefit the patient. Furthermore, such inappropriate use increases the risk of promoting drug-resistant bacterial strains. In a limited number of cases observed in one study, patients experienced a slight elevation in serum transaminase levels during treatment with methenamine hippurate tablets USP. However, these levels returned to normal even while the patients continued taking the medication. Based on this finding, it is advisable to periodically monitor liver function in patients receiving this drug, especially those with pre-existing liver dysfunction. The safety of methenamine hippurate tablets USP during early pregnancy has not been established. While its use in the last trimester appears to be safe, this has not been definitively proven. Animal studies involving pregnant rats and rabbits did not reveal any adverse effects on the fetus. However, it is important to note that methenamine hippurate tablets USP can interfere with laboratory tests measuring urine estriol levels during pregnancy. This interference, which results in unmeasurably low estriol values, occurs when acid hydrolysis is used in the testing process due to the presence of methenamine and/or formaldehyde in the urine. Switching to enzymatic hydrolysis instead of acid hydrolysis can resolve this issue. Patients should be informed that antibacterial drugs, including methenamine hippurate tablets USP, are only effective against bacterial infections and do not treat viral infections, such as the common cold. When prescribed for a bacterial infection, patients should be advised to adhere strictly to the prescribed dosage and complete the full course of therapy, even if they begin to feel better early in the treatment. Skipping doses or failing to complete the therapy can reduce the effectiveness of the treatment and increase the risk of bacteria developing resistance, rendering methenamine hippurate tablets USP or other antibacterial drugs less effective in the future. Clinical studies of methenamine hippurate have not included a sufficient number of participants aged 65 and older to determine whether their response differs from that of younger individuals. However, other clinical experiences have not identified significant differences in responses between elderly and younger patients. In general, dosing for elderly patients should be approached with caution, typically starting at the lower end of the dosing range. This is due to the higher likelihood of reduced hepatic, renal, or cardiac function, as well as the presence of other medical conditions or concurrent drug therapies in this population. Methenamine hippurate is contraindicated in patients with renal insufficiency.
